summary: A humorous tour of fictional seasonal festivals and agricultural myths, prompted by Professor Martha Haywood's 2023 compendium "Festive Follies." Each town's celebration, from pumpkin parades to turnip tossing and maize mazes, is paired with a local legend and a tongue-in-cheek expert comment. The note stresses that the tales should be taken with a pinch of salt while noting they foster community.
one_line: A playful survey of invented seasonal festivals and farming myths across imaginary towns, each with a comic expert rebuttal.
key_facts: Professor Martha Haywood of the University of Imaginaria revealed her compendium "Festive Follies: A Look at Seasonal Festivals and their Associated Myths" on September 1st, 2023.
The Great Pumpkin Parade is held in Ember Grove on October 12th, 2023; old-timer Jeb McDougle says pumpkins left under a harvest moon will waltz around the field.
Anthropologist Jenna Fischer calls the Great Pumpkin Parade "a community's poetic way of expressing their bond with the earth's cycles."
The village of Coldsnap holds the "Fiesta of the Fertile Frosty" every December 5th; legend says a snowman with a carrot nose, button eyes and a scarf brings cash.
89-year-old Sylvia Knitworth claims she finds loose change in her couch after building a Frosty, while economists remain skeptical.
Bountifields holds the "Dancing Scarecrow Gala" on April 15th, with human-sized scarecrows in flamboyant attire; Mayor Bethany O'Reilly says the crops would grow better out of jealousy.
Plant psychologist Dr. Reed Greenstalk says "Happy farmers make for happy plants."
On June 21st, the villagers of Sunnydale defend the Earth from solar flares with a sunrise sword fight using oven mitts and baguettes; Gunther Flex is the self-appointed solar guardian.
Solar physicist Emily Airheart notes that solar flares can't reach the Earth's surface.

RootsVille holds the "Turnip Tussle" on August 7th, hurling turnips to promote fertility; Arnold Yarrow is a three-time Turnip Toss Champion and horticulturalist Sandra Spade says it does turn the soil a bit.
In Aromatown on September 16th at midnight, people sing to plants, especially lavenders; vocalist Lila Melodia leads, and botanist Tim Root says plants "respond to vibrations."
On October 31st in Cornucopia Town, navigating the Maize Mazes by moonlight is believed to ensure a season free from earworms, according to shaman Willow Bark.
